extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, media researchers, and general readers interested in news selection
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and explanatory guidance on how journalists and editors decide which events are reported and how they are presented; a catalog of classical and contemporary 'news values' (timeliness, proximity, conflict, prominence, shareability, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that occur suddenly and fit well with the news organization's schedule are more likely to be reported than those that occur gradually or at inconvenient times of day or night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term trends are not likely to receive much coverage; suddenness and fit with production schedules increase newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that have only just happened, are current, ongoing, or are about to happen are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freshness of an event increases its chance of selection; timeliness is a core classic news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity / Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: To do with people or places close to the target audience; includes geographical and cultural proximity (also linked to meaningfulness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local events affecting communities directly are more likely to be covered because they are immediately understandable; cultural proximity (shared language, appearance, preoccupations) increases coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news (disasters, crimes, adverse developments) is more newsworthy than good news; sometimes described as 'the basic news value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negativity increases both selection and placement; however, some research also identifies Positivity as a value in specific domains (sports, science, feel‑good stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The converse of negativity: good news can be a distinct news value, notably in sports, science, and feel‑good tabloid stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harcup and O'Neill note that 'good news' can attract attention and shape editorial choices alongside bad news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition of people or forces resulting in a dramatic effect; events involving disagreement, tension, or opposition are especially newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict often yields dramatic, urgent, repeated coverage (wars, protests, political fights) and allows persuasive or adversarial framing by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are out of the ordinary, unexpected, or rare are more newsworthy than routine, unsurprising events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rarity and deviation from routine make a story attract attention; note tension with 'consonance' (media readiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events whose implications are clear make for better copy than those open to more than one interpretation or requiring complex background knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear cause–effect or straightforward implications help reporters and audiences; ambiguous events are harder to turn into accessible news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that can be portrayed as the actions of individuals will be more attractive than ones without a human-centred angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that can be contextualized in personal terms (affecting specific ordinary people) are more engaging than generalized accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness / Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience's sense of identification with the topic; cultural proximity and relevance to readers' own lives makes an event newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance is judged by how close an event is to target readers/viewers’ experiences; this increases perceived impact and selection probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: An event's consequences (on the target audience or others); events with significant consequences (high impact) are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-impact events attract coverage because of their effects; 'impact' is a general measure of an event's importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness (Attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events concerned with global powers or the rich, powerful, famous and infamous receive more attention; also includes the eliteness of sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories involving prominent actors or authoritative sources are more likely to be selected and trusted; sometimes called 'attribution' when focusing on sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflects the importance of certain individuals, groups or institutions; well-known figures and high-visibility events are more likely to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominence interacts with other values (e.g., a large-scale conflict involving notable figures is prioritized); modern updates emphasize celebrity and high-visibility coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events with a large scale, scope, or high intensity are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records, extremes and superlative quantities or intensities (largest, deadliest, most expensive) increase news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that fit with the media's expectations and preconceptions receive more coverage than those that defy them; relates to editors' stereotypes and mental scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consonance refers to media readiness to report an item (conflicts with 'unexpectedness' but concerns preparedness and fit with preconceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A story that is already in the news gathers inertia; ongoing stories keep attracting coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because organizations are already set up to report and public familiarity reduces ambiguity, continuity favors follow-up reporting and updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must compete for space; editors seek balance among different types of coverage so prominence depends on a story's relation to other competing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition is about the placement and proportion of stories in an edition or program; a surplus of one type of news can displace others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or professional competition between media may lead journalists to endorse the news value given to a story by a rival outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rival coverage can elevate items; newsrooms may follow competitors’ leads to avoid being scooped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-option
rubrics_metrics.description: A marginally newsworthy story may be covered if it relates to a major running story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking lesser items to prominent narratives increases their chance of selection (e.g., a side-issue attached to an ongoing scandal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: A marginal story that is already written and available may be selected ahead of a more newsworthy story that requires fresh research and writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-prepared copy or ready-to-publish material can displace more important but time-consuming reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is more likely to be covered if it has been pre-scheduled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planned events (press conferences, scheduled votes) are favored because they are easier to plan coverage for and fit production rhythms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story impact / Shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of a published story — whether it is being shared widely, read, liked, commented-on — affects its news value; shareable stories tend to be simple, emotional, unexpected and triggered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the digital age editors track analytics; stories likely to generate clicks and social engagement may receive more attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional media have strict deadlines and short production cycles, selecting for items that can be researched and covered quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that can be produced within tight deadlines are more likely to appear; this influences selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to deploy and control production and reporting staff and the functionality of technical resources can determine whether a story is covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical considerations (access, staff, equipment) can limit coverage even for otherwise newsworthy events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data / Facticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Media need to back up stories with data to remain reliable; reporters prefer raw data to take an unbiased perspective. An alternative term used is 'facticity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of verifiable facts and figures strengthens a story's newsworthiness, particularly in hard news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity between event and story values
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between values that relate to events (e.g., Eliteness, Proximity) and those that relate to the news story/product (e.g., Composition, Co-option).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors consider both event-intrinsic news values and how stories fit into the publication or program; this distinction affects placement and selection strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Perception / Risk Signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences may interpret news as a 'risk signal' — characterized by an element of change (uncertainty) and relevance to individual security — which drives interest and newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and publicists may manipulate perceived change and relevance (security concern) to maximize a story's strength; perceived threat to peace, prosperity or wellbeing often becomes headline news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security Concern / Boundary of Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The news value of a story, as interest for an audience, is determined by degree of change and the relevance that change has for the individual or group; beyond a 'boundary of relevance' change is no longer perceived as newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security concern is proportional to relevance for individual, family, social and societal groups; this boundary can be manipulated by communicators to include/exclude groups from audience concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Usefulness Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions of newsworthiness can be contaminated by political usefulness: individuals tend to view stories that provide 'ammunition' for their political views as more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cognitive bias affects both audience and potentially newsroom judgement of what merits coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary / Psychological sensitivity to negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological/evolutionary mechanisms make humans more attentive to negative stimuli; negative news tends to be processed faster and remembered better, influencing news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brain's responsiveness to negative stimuli (and gender differences discussed in literature) helps explain why negative framing is prevalent, though scholars urge caution about overgeneralizing evolutionary claims.
